title: Pods & Deployments: A Kubernetes Field Handbook
summary: A dense, practical study-notes series on how Kubernetes actually runs your containers: Pod anatomy and lifecycle, ReplicaSet reconciliation, Deployment rolling updates and rollbacks, the three probe types, and how requests/limits drive scheduling, QoS, throttling and eviction. Ends with a debug playbook and a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Why Pods Exist
points: Definition: a Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — one or more containers that are always co-scheduled onto the same node and share a lifecycle.
Kubernetes never schedules a bare container; the Pod is the scheduling atom. You scale Pods, not containers.
Shared namespaces inside a Pod: network namespace (same IP, same port space, containers reach each other on localhost) and IPC namespace; PID namespace is optional via shareProcessNamespace.
NOT shared by default: the filesystem. Containers share data only through explicitly mounted volumes (e.g. emptyDir).
Every Pod gets one routable cluster IP; two containers in the same Pod cannot both bind port 8080.
The pause (infra) container holds the network namespace open so app containers can crash and restart without the Pod losing its IP.
Pods are mortal and never resurrected: a deleted Pod is gone forever, and a replacement gets a new name and a new IP. Never hardcode Pod IPs — use a Service.
One-container-per-Pod is the normal case; multi-container Pods are for helpers that must share the network or disk (log shipper, proxy, config reloader).
Minimal Pod manifest: apiVersion: v1, kind: Pod, spec.containers[].{name, image, ports}.
You almost never write a bare Pod in production — bare Pods are not rescheduled if the node dies. Use a controller (Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet/Job).
Pod specs are largely immutable after creation: only image, resources (with in-place resize), activeDeadlineSeconds and tolerations can be changed; everything else requires replacing the Pod.

chapters.title: Pod Anatomy: Init, App, Sidecar
points: initContainers run to completion, one at a time, in order, before any app container starts. Use for schema migrations, waiting on a dependency, fetching secrets or config.
If an init container fails, the kubelet restarts it per the Pod's restartPolicy; the Pod stays in Init:Error / Init:CrashLoopBackOff and no app container ever starts.
Init containers can have different images and higher privileges than app containers — a common way to keep a hardened runtime image slim.
Sidecar pattern: a helper container running alongside the app for the whole Pod lifetime (Envoy proxy, fluent-bit log tailer, cloud-sql-proxy).

Native sidecars (Kubernetes 1.29+ GA): an initContainer with restartPolicy: Always — it starts before app containers, keeps running, and shuts down after them. Fixes the old Job-never-completes-because-the-sidecar-never-exits problem.
Ambassador pattern (sidecar proxies outbound traffic) vs adapter pattern (sidecar reshapes the app's output, e.g. metrics format) — same mechanism, different intent.
emptyDir volume is the standard channel between containers in a Pod; it lives and dies with the Pod, not with a single container restart.
Container ordering caveat: app containers start in spec order but Kubernetes does NOT wait for one to be ready before starting the next. Ordering guarantees come only from init containers.
Pod-level fields worth knowing: nodeSelector, affinity, tolerations, topologySpreadConstraints, securityContext, serviceAccountName, terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
Example: init container running `until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 2; done` to gate startup on the database being reachable.
Anti-pattern: cramming unrelated services into one Pod because 'they talk to each other'. If they can scale or fail independently, they belong in separate Pods behind Services.

chapters.title: Pod Lifecycle & Restart Policy
points: The five Pod phases: Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown. Phase is a coarse summary, not the whole truth.
Pending means accepted but not fully running — usually unschedulable (no node fits the resource request) or still pulling the image.
Pod conditions carry the detail: PodScheduled, Initialized, ContainersReady, Ready. `Ready` is what a Service uses to decide whether to send traffic.
Container states: Waiting (with a reason like ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff), Running, Terminated (with exitCode and reason like OOMKilled, Error, Completed).
restartPolicy is set on the Pod, applies to all containers: Always (default, required for Deployments), OnFailure, Never.
CrashLoopBackOff is not an error state, it's a back-off timer: the kubelet retries with exponential backoff 10s, 20s, 40s … capped at 5 minutes, reset after 10 minutes of successful running.
Termination sequence: Pod marked Terminating → removed from Service endpoints → preStop hook runs → SIGTERM to PID 1 → wait terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30) → SIGKILL.
Race condition to know: endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, so in-flight requests can hit a dying Pod. A `preStop: sleep 5` is the standard workaround.
Your app must handle SIGTERM. Shell-form CMD (`CMD npm start`) makes /bin/sh PID 1, which swallows SIGTERM — use exec form or an init like tini.
Exit code cheatsheet: 0 clean, 1 app error, 137 = 128+9 SIGKILL (usually OOMKilled or grace period expired), 143 = 128+15 SIGTERM.
`kubectl describe pod` Events section and `kubectl logs --previous` are the two first commands for any lifecycle mystery.

chapters.title: ReplicaSets & the Reconcile Loop
points: A ReplicaSet has one job: keep exactly N Pods matching its selector running, right now.
The control loop: observe actual state (list Pods by selector) → compare to spec.replicas → create or delete the difference → repeat forever. This is level-triggered, not edge-triggered.
Level-triggered means the controller reacts to the current state, not to events. A missed event self-heals on the next sync; a dropped message never causes permanent drift.
Three key fields: spec.replicas, spec.selector (matchLabels/matchExpressions), spec.template (the Pod template).
The selector must match the template's labels or the API server rejects the ReplicaSet — otherwise it would spawn Pods forever that it can't see.
Adoption: a ReplicaSet claims any existing Pod whose labels match its selector and that has no controller ownerReference. This is why overlapping selectors across ReplicaSets are dangerous.
ownerReferences on the Pod point back to the ReplicaSet; cascading delete of the ReplicaSet garbage-collects the Pods via that reference.
`kubectl delete rs my-rs --cascade=orphan` leaves the Pods running and unowned — occasionally useful for surgery.
Scale-down victim ordering (heuristic): Pending before Running, not-Ready before Ready, newer before older, higher-restart-count before lower, and Pods on nodes with more replicas first.
controller.kubernetes.io/pod-deletion-cost annotation lets you bias which Pods get removed first on scale-down (lower cost = deleted first).
ReplicaSet replaced the older ReplicationController; the only real difference is set-based selector support (matchExpressions with In/NotIn/Exists).
You should not create ReplicaSets directly — a Deployment creates and manages them for you, and that's where rollout logic lives.

chapters.title: Deployments: The Layer That Rolls
points: Ownership chain: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod. The Deployment manages ReplicaSets; each ReplicaSet manages Pods.
One ReplicaSet per unique Pod template. Changing the template creates a NEW ReplicaSet and scales the old one down — that IS the rolling update.
The pod-template-hash label is computed from the template and added to the ReplicaSet selector and Pod labels, so generations never claim each other's Pods.
Changing spec.replicas alone does NOT create a new ReplicaSet — scaling and rolling out are different operations.
Deployment status fields: replicas, updatedReplicas, readyReplicas, availableReplicas, unavailableReplicas. `available` ≠ `ready`: available means ready for at least minReadySeconds.
revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) controls how many old, scaled-to-zero ReplicaSets are kept for rollback. Set to 0 and you lose rollback ability.
progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) marks the Deployment Progressing=False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded if the rollout makes no headway — it does NOT auto-rollback.
`kubectl rollout status deploy/x` blocks until the rollout succeeds or hits the progress deadline — the canonical CI/CD gate.
Declarative update methods: `kubectl apply -f`, `kubectl set image deploy/x c=img:v2`, `kubectl edit`. All mutate the template and trigger the same machinery.
kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration is how `apply` computes a three-way merge patch; mixing `apply` with `edit`/`patch` is how fields mysteriously come back.
Deployments are for stateless workloads. Stable identity or per-Pod storage → StatefulSet. One Pod per node → DaemonSet. Run-to-completion → Job/CronJob.
Annotation kubernetes.io/change-cause (with `--record` deprecated) is what shows up in `kubectl rollout history`; set it yourself for readable history.

chapters.title: Rolling Updates: The Arithmetic
points: strategy.rollingUpdate has exactly two knobs: maxSurge and maxUnavailable. Both accept an absolute number or a percentage of spec.replicas.
Defaults are 25% / 25%, rounded: maxSurge rounds UP, maxUnavailable rounds DOWN.
Two hard invariants during the rollout: total Pods ≤ replicas + maxSurge, and available Pods ≥ replicas − maxUnavailable.
Worked example — replicas=10, maxSurge=25%, maxUnavailable=25%: ceil(2.5)=3 surge, floor(2.5)=2 unavailable → at most 13 Pods exist, at least 8 stay available.
Worked example — replicas=4, 25%/25%: surge=ceil(1)=1, unavailable=floor(1)=1 → cap 5 Pods, floor 3 available.
Worked example — replicas=2, 25%/25%: surge=ceil(0.5)=1, unavailable=floor(0.5)=0 → surge-only rollout, no capacity dip. This is why small Deployments feel slower but safer.
maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 = zero-capacity-loss rollout, one new Pod at a time. Slowest and safest; requires spare cluster capacity.
maxSurge: 0 with maxUnavailable: 1 = no extra capacity needed, but you run below full strength. Required when a quota or a fixed license count blocks extra Pods.
maxSurge and maxUnavailable cannot BOTH be 0 — the rollout could never make progress, and the API rejects it.

minReadySeconds gates the whole thing: a new Pod isn't counted available until it has been Ready continuously for that long, so the rollout waits. This catches Pods that are ready then immediately crash.
The step loop: scale new RS up to the surge cap → wait for availability → scale old RS down to the unavailable floor → repeat until new=replicas and old=0.

Readiness probes are what make rolling updates safe. With no readiness probe, a container is 'ready' the moment it starts, and the rollout marches on while every new Pod is still booting — a rolling outage.

chapters.title: Pause, Resume, Rollback, History
points: `kubectl rollout pause deploy/x` freezes the rollout mid-flight; further spec edits accumulate without triggering ReplicaSets. Batch several changes into one rollout this way.
`kubectl rollout resume deploy/x` applies all accumulated changes as a single new revision.
A paused Deployment still honors scaling — `kubectl scale` works while paused, but no template changes roll out.
`kubectl rollout undo deploy/x` reverts to the previous revision; `--to-revision=N` targets a specific one.
Rollback is not a rewind: it re-applies the old Pod template as a NEW revision number, scaling the old ReplicaSet back up. History moves forward, never backward.
Because the old ReplicaSet object still exists at replicas=0, rollback is fast — no image pull dance for cached images, just scale up.
`kubectl rollout history deploy/x --revision=3` prints that revision's full Pod template — the fastest way to diff what changed.

`kubectl rollout restart deploy/x` patches a kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt annotation into the template, forcing a fresh rolling restart with no image change. Use it to pick up a rotated Secret/ConfigMap.
Failed rollouts do NOT self-heal. If new Pods crashloop, the Deployment stalls with old Pods still serving — good (no outage) and bad (silently stuck). Watch for ProgressDeadlineExceeded.
Gotcha: rolling back a Deployment does not roll back the ConfigMap, Secret, or database migration it depended on. Version your ConfigMaps or your rollback is a lie.
revisionHistoryLimit: 0 disables `rollout undo` entirely — a surprisingly common self-inflicted wound.
CI pattern: `kubectl apply` → `kubectl rollout status --timeout=5m` → on non-zero exit, `kubectl rollout undo`.

chapters.title: Strategies Compared
points: RollingUpdate (default): gradual replacement, zero downtime, but two versions run simultaneously — your app and its schema must tolerate N and N+1 at once.
Recreate: kill all old Pods, then start new ones. Guaranteed single version, guaranteed downtime. Use for apps that can't run two copies (exclusive file lock, incompatible migration, single-writer).
Comparison row — downtime: Rolling = none, Recreate = full, Blue-Green = none, Canary = none.
Comparison row — extra capacity needed: Rolling = maxSurge worth, Recreate = none, Blue-Green = 2×, Canary = ~1.1×.
Comparison row — versions live at once: Rolling = 2 (uncontrolled mix), Recreate = 1, Blue-Green = 2 (only one receiving traffic), Canary = 2 (weighted).
Comparison row — rollback speed: Rolling = minutes (another rollout), Recreate = minutes + downtime, Blue-Green = instant (flip the Service selector), Canary = instant (shift weight to 0).
Comparison row — blast radius of a bad build: Rolling = grows as the rollout proceeds, Recreate = 100% immediately, Blue-Green = 0% until the flip then 100%, Canary = bounded to the canary share.
Blue-Green with vanilla Kubernetes: two Deployments (app-blue, app-green), one Service; flip by patching the Service's label selector. Atomic, no in-flight mixing.
Poor-man's canary with vanilla Kubernetes: two Deployments sharing a common Service selector label, replica counts 9 and 1 — traffic splits ~90/10 by Pod count, not by real weighting.
Real traffic-weighted canary needs an ingress/mesh (NGINX canary annotations, Istio VirtualService, Gateway API HTTPRoute weights) or a controller like Argo Rollouts / Flagger.
Deployments have no built-in automatic rollback on metrics. Progressive-delivery controllers add analysis steps that abort on error-rate or latency SLOs.

Decision rule: default to RollingUpdate; Recreate when concurrency is unsafe; Blue-Green when you need an instant, atomic revert; Canary when the risk is unknown and you have observability to judge it.

chapters.title: Probes I: The Three Kinds
points: Liveness probe answers 'is this container wedged?' On failure the kubelet KILLS and restarts the container. Wrong answer = restart loop.
Readiness probe answers 'should this Pod get traffic?' On failure the Pod's IP is removed from Service endpoints; the container keeps running.
Startup probe answers 'has this slow app finished booting?' While it's failing, liveness and readiness probes are suspended entirely.
Four handler types: httpGet (2xx/3xx = pass), tcpSocket (connection opens = pass), exec (exit 0 = pass), and grpc (standard gRPC health checking protocol).
exec probes are the most expensive — they fork a process in the container on every period. At period 5s across 1000 Pods that's real CPU.
Timing fields: initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds (default 10), timeoutSeconds (default 1), successThreshold (default 1, must be 1 for liveness/startup), failureThreshold (default 3).
Time to first restart = initialDelaySeconds + periodSeconds × failureThreshold (roughly). Compute it; don't guess.
Startup probe budget = failureThreshold × periodSeconds. e.g. 30 × 10s = 5 minutes of grace, then it kills the container. Startup probes replace huge initialDelaySeconds guesses.
httpGet probes come from the kubelet on the node, NOT through the Service, and by default do not follow redirects. host defaults to the Pod IP.
Probe endpoints should be unauthenticated, cheap, and on the app's own port. A probe path behind auth middleware returns 401 = permanent failure.
Readiness probes matter during shutdown too: failing readiness is how a Pod drains before SIGTERM.
Example: startupProbe httpGet /healthz failureThreshold 30 period 10; livenessProbe httpGet /healthz period 10 failureThreshold 3; readinessProbe httpGet /ready period 5.

chapters.title: Probes II: Tuning & Failure Modes
points: The #1 probe mistake: liveness and readiness pointing at the SAME endpoint that checks downstream dependencies.
Why that's fatal: the database blips → every Pod's liveness fails → the kubelet restarts every Pod at once → the whole Deployment cascades into CrashLoopBackOff while the DB is still down.
Correct split: liveness = shallow, checks only 'my process/event loop is alive'. Readiness = may check dependencies. Liveness must NEVER check a database or another service.
timeoutSeconds defaults to 1 second. Under GC pause or CPU throttling a healthy app easily misses that — spurious restarts blamed on 'flaky Kubernetes'.
CPU-limit interaction: a throttled container responds slowly, fails liveness, gets killed, restarts, gets throttled again. Restart-loop root cause is often the CPU limit, not the probe.
Too-aggressive liveness (period 1s, failureThreshold 1) turns a transient hiccup into an outage. Liveness should be forgiving; readiness can be twitchy.
No readiness probe at all = traffic hits Pods that are still warming their cache or JIT — 502s for the first N seconds of every rollout.
Readiness flapping causes endpoint churn, which propagates to kube-proxy/iptables on every node. Use successThreshold > 1 to require sustained recovery.
Startup probe failure kills the container per restartPolicy — it's a hard boot deadline, not just a delay.
Probes do not run against init containers, and probe failures during Pod termination are ignored.
Debug workflow: `kubectl describe pod` → look for 'Liveness probe failed:' events with the actual response, then reproduce with `kubectl exec -- curl -sv localhost:8080/healthz`.
Rule of thumb: liveness period 10s / timeout 3-5s / failureThreshold 3; readiness period 5s / timeout 2s; startup sized to worst-case cold start × 2.

chapters.title: Requests & Limits: Two Different Machines
points: requests are for the SCHEDULER — how much capacity to reserve when picking a node. limits are for the KERNEL (cgroups) on that node — the hard ceiling at runtime.
The scheduler only ever looks at requests, and it sums the requests of Pods already on the node, not their actual usage. A node can be 'full' at 20% real utilization.
CPU units: 1 = one core/vCPU/hyperthread. 500m = 0.5 core. Memory units: Mi/Gi are binary (1Mi = 1048576 bytes), M/G are decimal — mixing them is a classic 5% error.
CPU is compressible: exceeding the CPU limit throttles you (CFS quota), it never kills you. Memory is incompressible: exceeding the memory limit gets you OOMKilled, exit 137.
CPU requests map to cgroup cpu.shares — a relative weight during contention. On an idle node you can freely use more than your request.
CPU limits map to CFS quota/period (default 100ms period). Throttling happens per 100ms window, so a bursty app can be throttled while its average usage sits well below the limit.
Memory requests are essentially only a scheduling hint plus an eviction-ranking input; they do not reserve physical pages.
Set requests from observed p50–p90 usage; set memory limit near the request, and think hard before setting a CPU limit at all.

The 'no CPU limits' argument: CPU is compressible and shares already provide fairness under contention, so limits mostly buy you latency spikes. The counterargument: limits make performance predictable and prevent one noisy tenant from eating burst capacity.
Omitting requests entirely is the worst option: the Pod lands in BestEffort QoS and is first to be evicted, and the scheduler cannot make sane placement decisions.
LimitRange sets namespace defaults and min/max per Pod/container; ResourceQuota caps total requests/limits per namespace. A ResourceQuota on a namespace makes requests/limits mandatory.
VPA recommends or sets values from history; HPA scales replica count off utilization measured against the REQUEST — so a wrong request silently miscalibrates your autoscaler.

chapters.title: QoS, Eviction & OOMKills
points: Three QoS classes, assigned automatically, never set directly: Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort.
Guaranteed: every container has requests == limits for BOTH cpu and memory. Gets oom_score_adj -997, evicted last, and is eligible for exclusive CPUs under the static CPU manager policy.
Burstable: at least one container has a request, but requests != limits. The common, sensible default.
BestEffort: no requests and no limits anywhere in the Pod. Evicted first, killed first under node memory pressure.
Node-pressure eviction: the kubelet watches memory.available, nodefs.available, imagefs.available against eviction thresholds and evicts Pods to reclaim resources.
Eviction ranking: BestEffort first, then Burstable Pods exceeding their requests (ranked by how far over), then Guaranteed. Within a tier, higher Pod priority is evicted later.
Eviction is graceful (the Pod is terminated and rescheduled elsewhere). OOMKill is not — the kernel SIGKILLs the process instantly, no grace period, no preStop.
Container OOMKill vs node OOM: exceeding your own memory limit kills just that container (restarted in place); node-level memory exhaustion can kill processes based on oom_score_adj across Pods.
Diagnosing: `kubectl describe pod` shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137; the Pod's Events show Evicted with a message naming the pressure signal.

JVM/Node gotcha: runtimes that size their heap from the host's total memory rather than the cgroup limit will OOMKill instantly. Use container-aware flags (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage) and keep headroom for non-heap memory.
Preemption is different from eviction: a higher-PriorityClass Pending Pod causes the scheduler to evict lower-priority Pods to make room. Set PriorityClasses for critical workloads.

PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable / maxUnavailable) protects against VOLUNTARY disruption — node drains, cluster autoscaler scale-down. It does NOT protect against OOMKills, node crashes, or node-pressure eviction.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Debug Playbook
points: Pending forever → `kubectl describe pod`, read the FailedScheduling event: 'Insufficient cpu/memory' (request too big), 'didn't match node selector', or 'had untolerated taint'.
ImagePullBackOff → wrong tag, private registry with no imagePullSecrets, or rate-limited registry. `describe` shows the exact pull error.
CrashLoopBackOff → `kubectl logs pod --previous` for the dead container's output; check exit code 137 (OOM), 1 (app error), 143 (SIGTERM during shutdown).
Running but no traffic → the readiness probe is failing, or the Service selector doesn't match the Pod labels. Check `kubectl get endpoints <svc>`: empty endpoints is the tell.
Rollout stuck at 'Waiting for rollout to finish' → new Pods never become Ready. Look at the NEW ReplicaSet's Pods, not the Deployment.
Using `:latest` as the image tag: the template never changes, so `kubectl apply` triggers no rollout at all. Use immutable tags or digests; `rollout restart` if you must.

Mutating a ConfigMap without versioning it: mounted files update eventually (up to ~1 min sync), env vars never do, and nothing restarts. Version the ConfigMap name or add a checksum annotation to the Pod template.
Setting replicas in a manifest that HPA also manages: every `kubectl apply` fights the autoscaler. Remove spec.replicas from the manifest when an HPA owns it.
No PodDisruptionBudget + node drain = all replicas down at once during a cluster upgrade.
All replicas on one node because no topologySpreadConstraints or anti-affinity — a single node failure takes out the whole Deployment.
Copy-pasted resource values across every service ('1 CPU / 1Gi for everyone') wastes cluster capacity and throttles the services that actually need CPU. Measure, then set.

Useful commands: `kubectl get pods -o wide`, `kubectl describe pod/deploy/rs`, `kubectl logs -f --previous`, `kubectl top pod`, `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp`, `kubectl debug -it pod --image=busybox --target=app`.

chapters.title: One-Page Summary
points: The chain: you edit a Deployment → it creates a ReplicaSet per unique Pod template → the ReplicaSet reconciles Pod count → the kubelet runs containers and probes them.
Pod = scheduling atom, shares network + IPC, mortal, never rescheduled on its own. Always use a controller.
ReplicaSet = one level-triggered loop keeping N Pods alive, identified by the pod-template-hash label.
Deployment = ReplicaSet choreography: rolling updates, pause/resume, revision history, rollback.
Rolling update math: total ≤ replicas + maxSurge, available ≥ replicas − maxUnavailable; surge rounds up, unavailable rounds down; both zero is illegal.
Three probes, three jobs: liveness restarts (keep it shallow), readiness gates traffic (may check dependencies), startup buys boot time (suspends the other two).
requests = scheduler reservation; limits = kernel ceiling. CPU throttles, memory kills.
QoS falls out of your numbers: requests==limits everywhere → Guaranteed; some requests → Burstable; none → BestEffort and first to die.
Safe-rollout checklist: immutable image tag, readiness probe, minReadySeconds, maxUnavailable 0 if capacity allows, PDB, preStop sleep, SIGTERM handler, `rollout status` gate in CI.
Resource checklist: always set requests, set memory limit ≈ request, be deliberate about CPU limits, keep runtime heap under the cgroup limit, let HPA read a request you actually measured.
Fastest triage triad: `kubectl describe pod` (events), `kubectl logs --previous` (why it died), `kubectl get endpoints` (why no traffic).

Mental model to keep: Kubernetes is a set of controllers continuously driving observed state toward declared state. Every debugging question reduces to 'which controller is unhappy, and what does it see?'
